Posted August 20, 2004
Analysis by Richard Cowan

(MarijuanaNews note: In March of 2000, the cover article in Time Magazine trumpeted THE WORLD'S BEST POT NOW COMES FROM VANCOUVER. ". [The byline attributed the piece to Elaine Shannon in DC, who is listed as a contributor to this one.]
See
 Time Magazine Is Improving On The Party Line On " B. C. Bud. " Now it averages 30% THC! That is really B. S. Bud!

In my analysis I said,The best two-word explanation of marijuana prohibition is still " bad journalism. " This crap is an outstanding example, but inasmuch as Time pretends it is omniscient, this will be their received wisdom from now on.I have known for a few weeks that this article was in the works, because the Time reporter had talked to NORML National Director, Allen St. Pierre, longer than she had wanted to. It was immediately obvious to Allen that the reporter was preparing a party line piece, but he gave her the facts and referred her to various sources, including MarijuanaNews.

Major articles in Time are corporate efforts, the products of collective journalism, so this is no accident. It is now painfully obvious that the story was essentially already written in the Drug Czar's office, but at least we know that it is not the product of ignorance.

In fact, as one can see from the Time article four years ago, and the other stories linked below, there is no real news here. It is an old non-story that has been flogged for years by the prohibitionist establishment.

This Bud’s For the U.S.
Canada's relaxed drug laws may be fueling a boom in marijuana exports to America.
From Time Magazine
letters@time.com

By Anita Hamilton
Reported by Ben Bergman/Blaine, Laura Blue/New York, Chris Daniels/Toronto, Deborah Jones/Vancouver, and Elaine Shannon/Washington.
August 23, 2004 issue

It was the bus driver who noticed something suspicious. According to school officials, a driver for Blaine High School in northwestern Washington State thought something was strange about students' carrying unusually full bags to school and then never taking them back home. He alerted U.S. authorities, who boarded the bus on the morning of Feb. 20 and allegedly found 8 lbs. of marijuana, valued at $25,000, hidden inside a teenage girl's backpack. Prosecutors allege that the minor, 16, was getting paid $300 a trip to work as a drug mule for smugglers moving marijuana into the U.S. from Canada. The teen's home, in Point Roberts, Wash., borders British Columbia in an area with relatively light border patrol, which would have made it easy for her to get the drugs from Canada before getting on the bus.

Expelled from school and charged with possessing marijuana with intent to deliver, the girl has a hearing scheduled for Aug. 23 in Bellingham, Wash. Deputy prosecutor Thomas Verge has said he will probably ask for an exceptionally long sentence that would put the teen behind bars until her 21st birthday. The controversy has upset the community. " She was a wonderful young girl, " says her principal, Dan Newell. " I wouldn't have ever thought that if anyone was going to haul marijuana across the border, it would be this lady. "
(MarijuanaNews note: It is a journalistic cliché to begin news stories with a human interest hook like this, but the unintended consequence of this little tragedy is to demonstrate that the dehumanizing effect of the prohibitionist police state. Time seems to find it unobjectionable that a teenage girl would be sent to prison for years. The rest of the article would seem to prove that it would be pointless.

From another “human interest” perspective one might also notice that most of the reporters on this story are female, liberated women who have no difficulty lying to justify putting a girl in prison. You’ve come a long way, babies!)

Nor would anyone have thought that the cross-border traffic of illegal drugs would become one of the knottiest areas of disagreement between the U.S. and its northern neighbor. An estimated 880 to 2,200 tons of marijuana are grown in Canada, according to a new report from Canadian police.
(MarijuanaNews note: Actually, that is not quite right.

Here is what the RCMP say in their report, The Drug Situation in Canada 2003.For the last five years, Canadian law enforcement agencies seized annually an average of 1.1 million marihuana plants, a six-fold increase since 1993. Based on seizures and average yield per plant, the current annual production estimate could likely range between 800 and 2,000 metric tonnes. In previous years, the 800 tonne estimate was arrived at using a 25 percent seizure ratio. In 2003, it was decided to use a range estimate maintaining the 25 percent ratio for the low-end and a 10 percent seizure ratio for the high-end range (i.e. 2,000 tonnes). For some police forces, investigations into marihuana grow operations represent more than half of their drug cases. Perhaps Time added 10% to the Canadian numbers as a tip.)

About 90% of the commercial crop winds up in the U.S., where its street value ranges from $5 billion to $25 billion.
(MarijuanaNews note: One need not know anything about cannabis to wonder about these numbers.

First, if the guesstimates on volume ranges from 800 to 2000 tons, and market value ranges from $5 billion to $25 billion, how can we know that about 90% goes south, regardless of the volume? In fact, there is no official source for that number, even though John Walters has claimed that 95% of Canadian production goes South.

If 90% of the lower number, 800 tons, goes south then that would leave only 80 tons for the Canadian market. The Canadian population (31 million) is a little more than ten percent of the US (290 million), and less than California’s 34 million.

Consider the implication of these numbers. If Americans consume nine times as much Canadian cannabis as do the Canadians themselves, and as the next sentence tells us only 5% of pot in the U.S. comes from Canada, then Americans must consume almost twenty times as much cannabis per capita as do Canadians, despite having much harsher penalties. [To review: US population is roughly nine times that of Canada, so if Americans got all of their cannabis from Canada, which was 90% of Canadian production, then per capita consumption would be roughly equal, but if Canada supplies only 5% of the market, then Americans toke 20 times more weed. If one uses the higher estimate of 2,000 tons then US per capita consumption would be almost 100 times higher than Canada's. That is absurd, but so are Times numbers, and yet none of the editors at Time cared. After all it's only marijuana!]

The dollar amounts are even more confusing, because it is hard to know just how much BC Bud and US domestic sinsemilla really sell for. While BC Bud sells for a substantial premium over Mexican commercial, there is no reason that it should sell for more than US sinsemilla, marketing hype aside.

However, according to the Drug Czar’s own report, total US expenditures on marijuana in 2000 were only $11 billion dollars, so according to Time’s $25 billion estimate Canada may supply over 200% of the US market for marijuana in dollar terms.)

Although only 5% of pot in the U.S. comes from Canada, the trade is flourishing because of high demand in the U.S. and the comparatively mild punishments in Canada for growers and traffickers.

The U.S. seized more than 48,000 lbs. of marijuana along the Canadian border last year, nearly double the 26,000 lbs. it retrieved in 2002, according to a U.S. State Department report. There have been seizures all along the border, in Montana, North Dakota, Michigan, Ohio and other states.
(MarijuanaNews note: As noted above, that 5% number should have brought into question all of the other numbers in the article, and the whole premise of the article, but even that number is probably much too high.

Never mind that the RCMP report, The Drug Situation in Canada 2003, citesthe US Customs data saying that in 2003, 15,697 kg., or approximately 34,000 pounds, were seized at the Canadian border. The real questions are about the other 95%.

Meanwhile at the Mexican border the RCMP says US Customs data for 2003 showed that 406,203 kg or approximately 880,000 pounds were seized. Thus seizures of Canadian Bud were only about 4% of the seizures of Mexican weed. And seizures are the only hard data that we have. Everything else is just a guesstimate, at best.

And then there is US domestic production, which supposedly provides roughly half the US supply. That would mean that Canada probably supplies less than three percent of the total volume, but a higher percentage of the dollar value.

Unless

So Times numbers do not make any sense at all, unless the US marijuana market is vastly larger than the official estimate of $11 billion, which I think is more likely than not. Canada still would not be a major source of cannabis, but if the Canadian marijuana production is even close to the higher numbers, the US marijuana market must be huge indeed.

In any case, despite harsh laws, DEAland itself is the world's largest consumer, grower, and importer of cannabis. Now that would be a story, but it would make the Drug War look even more futile, and wrecking the life a teenage girl would be not only cruel but stupid.)

The featured brand is BC Bud which is grown in British Columbia and has become synonymous with the high-grade marijuana grown throughout Canada. Once in the U.S., the pot is exchanged for cash, and sometimes cocaine or guns, which are then smuggled back to Canada.
(MarijuanaNews note: Also not a new story, and there is no evidence that it happens with any frequency, but it sounds sooo good to a prohibitionist.

Although the actual potency of BC Bud varies from batch to batch, depending on how it's grown, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration says that as much as 25% of BC Bud is made of the psychoactive drug tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). In contrast, the pot that the hippie generation smoked in the 1970s had only 2% THC content, and most pot consumed in the U.S. today averages about 7% THC.
(MarijuanaNews note: Ah yes, the obligatory effort to make the reader think that the 60s were about a placebo. One more prohibitionist cliché.
From 1998, see
 Marijuana Prohibition And Potency, Price, And Safety --
" Is Marijuana Stronger Than It Was Back In the '60s, When Everyone Thought It Was Harmless? "

However, it is amusing that Time infallibly claims that BC Bud is only 25% THC whereas they told us infallibly that it was 30% THC four years ago. Actually, the DEA says, Canada is becoming a source country for indoor-grown, high-potency (15 to 25 percent THC) marijuana destined for the United States.

From http://www.usdoj.gov/dea/concern/drug_trafficking.html undated, but probably from 2001.

The DEA also acknowledges that there is no difference in BC Bud and US indoor cultivated cannabis. How could there be? The growing techniques are the same, as are the genetics. BC seed merchant Marc Emery says that 80% of his sales are to DEAland.

However, having cited the RCMP report plus 10% -- on the quantity of all Canadian Bud, Time then ignores what the same report says on potency:
From http://www.rcmp-grc.gc.ca/crimint/drugs_2003_e.htm#marihuana
THC (Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol) levels in Canada

For several years now, one of the most frequently reported aspects of marihuana production in Canada has been the Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, levels associated with Canadian marihuana. Increasingly, Canadian marihuana is being referred to as high-grade, with reported THC levels averaging 20 percent or more. It should be pointed out, however, that such statements are not quite accurate. According to Health Canada official laboratory analyses of marihuana (grown outdoor and indoor) samples since 1998, THC levels average 10 percent. One single marihuana exhibit in the last two-years did test at a THC level of 27 percent. However, the majority, or some 60 percent of exhibits, recorded THC levels of 9 percent or less, and 32 percent of exhibits had THC levels of between 10 percent and 14 percent.

In other words, Time misrepresents or ignores what the official sources actually say, even after citing them, so they know that they are lying. )

White House drug czar John Walters blames BC Bud in part for the increased number of pot-related emergency room incidents, which have more than doubled, from 54,000 in 1996 to 119,000 in 2002. Those incidents range from accidents and injuries to unexpected reactions to the drug. " Canada is exporting to us the crack of marijuana, " Walters told reporters in April.
(MarijuanaNews note: More prohibitionist than Walters? This grotesque mischaracterization of the emergency room data is even sleazier than the Czar's usual offerings. The emergency room data is about mentions of any illegal drug on a form that has places for five. It has nothing to do with the actual cause of the visit.

Only about 34,000 visits involve marijuana only mentions, and even then it may not be the cause of the visit. After all, doctors want to know what drugs a patient has been using legal or illegal so that they can know what drugs they can give to the patient.

But again, how could five percent of the marijuana cause a national increase in ER visits. To put this into context, which Time will not, there are approximately 100 million ER visits every year in the US. Alcohol accounts for roughly 25% of all emergency room visits. Marijuana mentions, even with every other drug including alcohol involved less than one tenth of one percent of such visits.

Others dispute Walters' claims. " Domestic American marijuana is probably a little bit better, " says Richard Stratton, editor in chief of High Times, a magazine that covers marijuana issues. But the BC Bud name is so well regarded that some dealers pass off other varieties as Canadian to fetch the $3,000-to-$10,000-per-lb. price.
(MarijuanaNews note: $3,000-to-$10,000-per-lb.?? Inflation. Even the DOJ says that it only sells for $5,000 and $8,000 per pound in major metropolitan areas.

Notice that the editor of High Times is the only anti-prohibitionist cited in the article, even though we know that the reporter talked to Allen St. Pierre at some length.

In Times Canadian edition, but not the American edition, there is a sidebar The Branding of BC Bud in which Allen is quoted on the same subject: Our government here has puffed up that product. That is it. That is all the anti-prohibitionists are allowed to say. Ah, balanced reporting.

Of course, Time chose to ignore Allen's explanation for the hype. It is the prohibitionist party line endlessly parroted by the prohibitionist media that has created the myth of BC Bud.
See

John Walters Testimony To The Canadian Parliament. The Public Record Or What He Would Have Said, If He Was Not Afraid of Being Asked Embarrassing Questions. The Battle for Canada.

Instead, it says, Still, the principal promoters of BC Bud are the ones who stand to make the most from it: dealers and growers working hard to market their product. Or could it be that the prohibitionists have a vested interest in the hype, and they do it for the power?)

And BC Bud seems to be everywhere. " It's hella easy to get, " says " Angelo, " 22, a Seattle resident who asked to be identified by a pseudonym. " You can usually go to [a convenience store] between 1:30 a.m. and 3:30 a.m. and ask people who you think smoke bud, " he says.
(MarijuanaNews note: They say that it is only 5% of the US market, but it seems to be everywhere. Neat trick. In fact, Washington state is listed by the DOJ as one of the top five producers of indoor marijuana. According to the Drug Czar's web site, The five leading states for indoor growing activity were California, Washington, Texas, Florida, and Michigan. Notice that two states are on the Canadian border and California is often cited as a major market for BC Bud.
See Bureau of Justice Statistics, Sourcebook of Criminal Justice Statistics Online

On the Canadian side, the drug is even more ubiquitous. At the popular New Amsterdam Cafe in downtown Vancouver, customers openly smoke marijuana. " People come with pot. We are a business, though, so we have a $2 minimum cafe charge [for snacks and drinks], " says cafe manager Scott Heardy. Inspector David Nelmes, who is in charge of drugs for the Vancouver police department, tells TIME, " I can't remember the last time a member of the Vancouver police department arrested someone for smoking a joint. Frankly, who's got time? " If passed within the year, as seems likely, new Canadian legislation would decriminalize possession of less than 15 grams of marijuana, meaning that offenders would be slapped with only the equivalent of a traffic ticket. That approach is a far cry from the one that is taken in U.S. states like Oklahoma, where a person caught smoking dope could get up to a year in prison, although probation is more common.
(MarijuanaNews note: Oklahoma??? One would think that an American magazine would know that 100 million Americans in 12 states live under some form of decriminalization including border states like New York and Maine. All of them have decrim for more than the 15 grams proposed in Canada. Ohio has a fine for 100 grams.)

Canada's attitude toward small-scale toking up has led some U.S. officials to blame the northerners for the influx of BC Bud in America.
(MarijuanaNews note: Now how would Canada's attitude toward possession increase the export of BC Bud. It should increase domestic Canadian demand and therefore decrease the volume available for export. Not that the laws have any impact on consumption levels.)

" If the perception is that it will be easier to get marijuana in Canada ... then it creates problems at the border, " Paul Cellucci, U.S. ambassador to Canada, said at a Toronto Board of Trade dinner in February.
See

Indeed, the trade has led to an increase in drive-by shootings in Canada by rival dealers, and to " grow-rips, " in which competing clans break into growers' houses to steal their crops, according to Canadian police. The body of the suspected ringleader of a trafficking group was found stabbed in the neck in a ditch in Coeur d'Alene, Idaho, in November 2002. " It's still a dangerous drug, " says James Capra, the DEA's chief of domestic operations. " People are killing each other over it. "
(MarijuanaNews note: Whereas alcohol is a safe drug because people don't kill each other over it. They just kill each other when they use it.)

Currently, a grower in Canada who has been convicted can expect less than two years of house arrest and a trafficker anywhere from three months to five years, served either at home or in prison, compared with the minimum punishment of five to 10 years that most convicted traffickers and growers receive in U.S. federal court.
(MarijuanaNews note: Notice that the reference is to federal courts, not to state courts where most cases are tried.)

But as the violence has increased and cultivation of the crop has moved into residential areas, Canada has begun cracking down on its estimated 50,000 commercial pot growers. Over the past four years, police in Vancouver have seized $288 million worth of marijuana and $8.7 million worth of growing equipment. In Barrie, Ont., in January, police confiscated 30,000 marijuana plants, worth $23 million, inside a former Molson brewery.

One hot, muggy morning in July, a TIME reporter accompanied the Vancouver police as an officer thumped on the door of a two-story brick-and-panel house on a leafy street of manicured lawns. Inside, officers discovered a basement filled wall to wall with more than 300 glossy female cannabis bushes. That bust is pretty routine, but the BC Bud keeps flowing. In the past four years, Vancouver police have made more than 1,500 others, or about one a day.
(MarijuanaNews note: The Canadian editionis a bit different. The RCMP's own data:

Export of Canadian Marihuana to the U.S.
The export of Canadian marihuana to the U.S. has become a thriving industry across Canada, particularly in BC, Ontario and Quebec. Seizures of marihuana going south, proceeds coming north, and cocaine coming north (purchased with marihuana proceeds) clearly support this trend. This industry has brought about an abundance of U.S. currency in Canada. Some marihuana traffickers are conducting black market currency exchange. Some also deal with unscrupulous currency exchange businesses that charge a premium to handle the transactions discreetly.

Despite the preceding, most of the marihuana available on the American illicit market still originates primarily in the U.S. and in Mexico. Canada ranks far below Mexico as a source for the U.S. The following comparative data of U.S. Customs seizure statistics (see below) put this situation into perspective.

U.S. Customs Marihuana Seizures
(Data provided by U.S. Customs in February 2004)

Marihuana Production in the United States
U.S. authorities continue to report that their primary source of marihuana remains the United States. Two recent reports on U.S. drug issues (the International Narcotics Control Strategy Report released by the Bureau for International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs, March 2004 and the National Drug Threat Assessment 2004 released by the US National Drug Intelligence Center), have tentatively estimated that there are approximately 10,000 metric tonnes of marihuana produced in the United States annually. There is a perception in the enforcement community that the greater portion (possibly over two thirds) of this marihuana is cultivated outdoors.

THC levels in the United States
The University of Mississippi conducts on an ongoing basis a Marihuana Potency Monitoring Program to determine THC levels in marihuana samples provided for analysis. From 2000 to 2003, commercial grade marihuana (U.S. general designation for marihuana cultivated outdoors) had an average of 4.91 percent while sinsemilla marihuana (designation for marihuana in bud form) averaged 11.28 percent of THC. The highest THC level obtained was 33percent from a sample from an Oregon case in 1997.
